fields.title: An external system as a product risk
fields.keyTakeaway: Every external dependency must have a pre-determined failure behavior, and a slow response is more dangerous than no response because without a timeout it drags our product down with it.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: The payment provider is down for twenty minutes. What do buyers see during this time, and what happens to revenue?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: The answer to this question is either designed in advance or improvised during an outage—and improvisation costs dearly. Twenty minutes of total checkout unavailability during an evening peak at Polka means about 900 orders, some of which will never return. Thoughtful degradation turns those twenty minutes into an inconvenience instead of a shutdown.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: An [[external-dependency|external dependency]] breaks in five ways, and only the first one is obvious.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: **Unavailability.** Doesn't respond at all. The most noticeable and simplest case.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: **Slowness.** Responds, but in ten seconds instead of three hundred milliseconds. More dangerous than a complete failure: our requests pile up, resources run out, and our system goes down instead. Hence the rule—every outbound call must have a [[timeout|timeout]], and a short one at that.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: **Contract changes.** Removed a field, changed the format. With a good provider—with a warning and a [[deprecation|deprecation period]], with a bad one—silently.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: **Rate limit exhaustion.** The [[rate-limit|limit]] or [[quota|quota]] runs out, and the external system returns `429`. Often occurs suddenly—during traffic spikes or due to a bug in our code creating extra calls.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: **Meaning changes.** The format is the same, the field's meaning is different. Nothing crashes, and this is discovered last of all.
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: For every dependency, the product needs a **[[fallback|fallback plan]]**—pre-determined failure behavior. There are few options:
fields.sections/2/blocks/7/text: *[[response-cache|Cache]].* We return the last known response. Suitable for reference data: catalog, categories. *[[graceful-degradation|Degradation]].* The product works in a trimmed-down mode. Checkout without bonuses if the bonus service is down. *Postpone.* Queue it up and execute later. Good for notifications, not for payment. *Honest refusal.* We state directly that it's temporarily unavailable and give a timeframe.
fields.sections/2/blocks/8/text: The question to ask for every integration at the design stage: **what does the product do if this service is gone for five minutes?** If the answer is "doesn't work at all"—that's a product decision, and it needs to be made consciously rather than discovered.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: Five dependencies and their fallback plans.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/rows/0/2: Cash-on-delivery checkout; if it fails too, an honest message with a timeframe
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/rows/1/2: Order placed, status "clarifying", will update later
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/rows/2/2: Cache of the last export, up to a day; date note on the item card
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/rows/3/2: Queue, send later; push as the main channel
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/rows/4/2: Checkout without points with an explanation, points awarded later
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: Cash on delivery appeared precisely as a fallback plan and turned out to be in demand on its own—it accounts for 7% of orders during normal times. A byproduct product outcome of fault-tolerance work.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: The slowness case was telling: the catalog supplier started responding in 40 seconds instead of one. There was no timeout, requests piled up, and after fifteen minutes the entire app stopped opening. Someone else's slowness brought down our product. A 3-second timeout added afterward cost an hour of work.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: A fallback plan only makes sense if it's tested. An untested backup path breaks right when it's needed because it was never used. Regular testing by disabling is a separate practice, and the first time it's run, it usually reveals that the fallback plan doesn't work.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: Every external dependency must have a pre-determined failure behavior, and a slow response is more dangerous than no response because without a timeout it drags our product down with it.
